beats.say: There's one number, set by nine people in London, that affects your mortgage, your rent, your savings, your job, and even the price of your shopping. It's the Bank of England's interest rate.

vis.text: One number. Nine people. Your whole financial life.

beats.say: If you understand this one number, you'll understand a huge amount about money. Let's break down what it is, who sets it, and how it reaches your pocket.
Part one. What is Bank Rate?

Bank Rate, often called the base rate, is the interest rate the Bank of England pays to commercial banks on money they hold with it. It's the foundation that most other interest rates in the UK are built on.

vis.text: The foundation of every other rate.

beats.say: It's set by the Monetary Policy Committee, a group of nine people, including the Governor of the Bank of England and independent experts. They meet eight times a year and vote.

vis.sub: Nine members, eight meetings a year

beats.say: Their main job is to keep inflation close to the government's target of two percent. When inflation is too high, they tend to raise rates. When the economy is weak and inflation is low, they tend to cut them.

Since nineteen ninety seven, the Bank of England has been independent in setting interest rates. Before that, the Chancellor of the Exchequer made the final decision, which meant politics could get mixed in.
Part two. How it reaches you.
When Bank Rate changes, banks change the rates they charge borrowers and pay savers. That changes how much people borrow and spend, which changes prices and jobs across the whole economy.
Think of it like a thermostat for the economy. Higher rates make borrowing expensive and saving more rewarding, so people spend less. Lower rates do the opposite.
Rate changes also affect the value of the pound. Higher rates can attract money from abroad, pushing the pound up, which makes imports cheaper and can help bring inflation down.
Part three. Your mortgage.

For many people, the biggest impact is their mortgage. On a tracker or variable mortgage, payments can change soon after Bank Rate changes. On a fixed rate, nothing changes until the deal ends. But then it can be a shock.

vis.text: Fixed deals end. Then comes the shock.

beats.say: Here's an example. On a two hundred thousand pound repayment mortgage over twenty five years, monthly payments are roughly eight hundred and fifty pounds at two percent interest, and roughly one thousand one hundred and seventy pounds at five percent.
That's hundreds of pounds a month, just from a change in interest rates. That's why rate decisions make headlines.
Mortgage lenders also stress test borrowers, checking whether they could still afford payments if rates rose. So higher rates can also reduce how much people are allowed to borrow.

vis.text: Higher rates can shrink how much you can borrow.

beats.say: Part four. Your rent, savings and job.

Even if you don't have a mortgage, rates still affect you. Landlords with mortgages may pass higher costs on through rent. Credit cards and loans get more expensive. And when businesses borrow less, they may hire less.
But higher rates are good news for savers. Banks usually pay more interest on savings accounts. After years of tiny returns, many savers saw much better rates when Bank Rate rose.
Part five. A rollercoaster.

Bank Rate has moved a lot in recent history. After the two thousand and eight crash, it was cut to record lows, and stayed low for years. In twenty twenty, during the pandemic, it fell to just zero point one percent. Then inflation surged, and rates rose quickly, reaching five point two five percent in twenty twenty three.
For people who'd only ever known very low rates, that rise was a big shock. Mortgage payments jumped for many families as their fixed deals ended.

vis.text: A generation used to cheap money got a shock.

beats.say: Since that peak, rates have moved again as inflation has changed. Because rates keep changing, it's always worth checking the current Bank Rate rather than relying on an old number.
Part six. Why not keep rates low forever?
If low rates make borrowing cheap, why not keep them low forever? Because cheap money can push up prices, including house prices, and fuel inflation. And very low rates punish savers.

vis.text: Cheap money has a price too.

beats.say: Setting rates is a balancing act. Too high, and you risk a recession and job losses. Too low, and you risk inflation getting out of control. And changes take time to work, often a year or two.
Part seven. What you can do.

You can't control interest rates. But you can prepare for them. Know whether your mortgage is fixed or variable, and when your deal ends. Shop around for savings rates. And avoid debts that could become unaffordable if rates rise.

vis.title: Be ready
items: Know when your fixed deal ends
Keep a buffer for rate rises

beats.say: Interest rates are the price of money. And when the price of money changes, everything else changes with it.

vis.text: Interest rates are the price of money.
